897.title: Rediscovery
897.hook: Western scholars begin reading the Pali texts, and a society forms to print them
897.howItsDone: Buddhist monks and lay readers chant and study the same verses for years, and many now read them alongside older and newer English translations, comparing how each one renders a line.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Dharmapala, the Sri Lankan layman who campaigned for Bodh Gaya and stood up to speak in Chicago. Your line: he spoke up. Today, people far away start listening.

A palm-leaf manuscript, its edges dark from handling, lies open on a table in a European library. The script is one the reader is still learning. For the monks who copied it in Sri Lanka or Burma, these words were nothing new. They had been chanted, taught and copied long before this reader was born. For the reader at that table, almost every line is a surprise. That gap is today's story. The teaching was never lost. It was being read by new eyes.
screen: `A PALM LEAF ON A LIBRARY TABLE.` → `OLD WORDS, NEW EYES.` → `NEVER LOST.`

segments.voice: Start with what rediscovery is not. Buddhists in Sri Lanka, Burma, Thailand and beyond did not need anyone to find their scriptures. Monks memorized them, copied them and taught them, teacher to student. What changed was who else was reading. As European scholars learned Pali and Sanskrit, they began to translate. Friedrich Max Müller put the Dhammapada into English. Thomas Rhys Davids, who had learned Pali while working in Sri Lanka, turned to the long discourses. He and others formed a society in London to print the Pali texts in Roman letters, for readers who couldn't read the old scripts. Some of those English versions are the ones this path quotes. Here is a line from Max Müller's Dhammapada: "For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love—this is an old rule." An old rule, read again in a new language. The work had its blind spots. Some early scholars treated living Buddhists as if they were footnotes to a dead book. Some Asian Buddhists, including Dharmapala, answered by teaching and publishing for themselves, and the conversation became two-way. And here is the turn: those translations are now old too. Readers today notice their stiff phrasing and their word choices. So rediscovery keeps happening. Each generation reads the same verses again and finds something the last one missed.

segments.voice: Say today's line once, slowly, under your breath: hatred does not cease by hatred; hatred ceases by love; this is an old rule. Bring it back on a few out-breaths, and notice one word that sounds old-fashioned and one that still lands. You don't have to decide what it means; just read it again, the way people have for a long time.
Rediscovery. The moment Western scholars began reading Buddhist texts that Buddhists had kept alive all along, and the way each generation reads them again.

898.title: The southern map
898.hook: India to Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Java
898.howItsDone: Theravada monks in Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia chant the Pali texts daily, and monks from these countries have long visited and ordained in one another's monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday: rediscovery, scholars far away reading texts Buddhists had kept all along. Your line: read again. Today, the whole map at once.

Put your finger on the plain of the Ganges, where the Buddha walked and taught. Slide it south, down the long coast of India, across a narrow strait to the island of Sri Lanka. Swing east across the Bay of Bengal to Myanmar. Keep going into Thailand, up the river to Laos, down into Cambodia, and out across the sea to the island of Java. For weeks this path has walked that line one place at a time. Today, the whole southern map at once.
screen: `THE GANGES PLAIN.` → `SOUTH TO THE ISLAND.` → `EAST ACROSS THE BAY.`

segments.voice: First stop, India, where it began: councils of monks gathering to keep the teaching straight, and an emperor, Ashoka, sending messengers outward. Second, Sri Lanka. The island's chronicles say Ashoka's son, the monk Mahinda, brought the teaching there, and a cutting of the Bodhi tree followed. The island became a keeper of the Pali texts. Third, the mainland: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia. Here the teaching traveled with monks, with traders, and with kings who built and gave. You've met Sukhothai's walking Buddhas, the smiling towers of Angkor, and the saffron line at dawn in Luang Prabang. Fourth, the sea road to Java, where Borobudur rose as a mountain of carved stone. Now notice what the map doesn't show. A line on a map looks like one clean journey. It wasn't. The teaching moved back and forth, over a long time. Monks from the mainland sailed to Sri Lanka to be ordained again, and carried the lineage home. Kings sent for texts and teachers. Some places took up other forms of Buddhism, and some, like Java, later took up other faiths. Today the Theravada tradition, the way of the elders, lives on in Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Laos and Cambodia, and its monks chant the same Pali texts. A monk in Colombo and a monk in Vientiane can recite the same verses in the same old language. That shared voice is the southern road.

899.title: After the Buddha, closed
899.hook: councils, an emperor, an island, a king's questions, a road south
899.howItsDone: Buddhist communities retell the history of the councils, Ashoka and Mahinda at festivals and in sermons, and in Sri Lanka the arrival of Mahinda is remembered each year at the Poson full moon.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Theravada and the southern road, from India to Sri Lanka and across to Java. Your line: the southern road. Today, this whole stretch of the story closes.

When a teacher dies, the students face a plain question: now what? The Buddha's own last words, in the Pali account, put the work back in their hands. Decay is part of all compound things, he said; keep striving, with care. Then he was gone, and the teaching had no founder in the room. Everything in this part of the path, from the monks gathering to recite to the saffron line in Laos, answers that question. Today, the whole answer.
screen: `NOW WHAT?` → `KEEP STRIVING, WITH CARE.` → `THE WHOLE ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Five pieces. First, the councils. Monks gathered to recite together what the Buddha had taught, so the words were kept by many mouths instead of one memory. Later councils argued over the rules, and the community began to divide into schools. Second, an emperor. Ashoka, after a bloody war, carved edicts in stone about restraint and kindness, and sent messengers out from India. Third, an island. In Sri Lanka, the chronicles say, Ashoka's son Mahinda brought the teaching, and the island's monks went on to write the Pali texts down. Fourth, a king's questions. In the Questions of King Milinda, a Greek-born king asks the monk Nagasena hard things: if there is no lasting self, who is talking to me? Nagasena answers with a chariot. Is the chariot the wheels? The axle? The pole? None of them alone, and yet the word chariot works. The king is satisfied, and the conversation goes on. Fifth, the road south: Myanmar, Thailand, Laos, Cambodia, Java, with monks, traders and kings carrying it from port to port. Put the five together and one thing stands out. The teaching survived by moving. Every time it was recited, written, carved or carried, it reached someone new, and they shaped it too. The whole stretch in a sentence: it traveled. Tomorrow it turns north.

900.title: The Silk Road
900.hook: monks traveled with merchants along the caravan roads into Central Asia and China
900.howItsDone: Buddhist monks have long depended on lay supporters for food and shelter, and merchants and business owners are often among the donors who support monasteries.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the southern story: councils, an emperor, an island, a king's questions about the chariot. Your line: it traveled. Today a new stretch begins, on the northern roads.

Dust, bells and the slow sway of camels. A caravan winds between desert and mountain, loaded with cloth, spices and silver. Near the back, in robes the color of the dust, walk a few monks. They carry almost nothing: a bowl, a few manuscripts, a teaching memorized by heart. The merchants are glad of them. Monks bless the journey, and some merchants give food and shelter in return. At the oasis towns along the way, small monasteries begin to appear. The northern road is open: the Silk Road.
screen: `A CARAVAN IN THE DUST.` → `MONKS AT THE BACK.` → `MONASTERIES AT THE OASES.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Silk Road is a modern label for a web of caravan routes, not one road, running from the edges of India and Persia, through Central Asia, into China. Goods moved along it, and so did ideas. Second, traders were in the story from the start. The Vinaya, the monks' rulebook, tells of two merchants, Tapussa and Bhallika, traveling with a caravan, who met the Buddha soon after his awakening, offered him food, and took refuge in him and his teaching. Third, the oasis towns. Places like Khotan and Kucha, ringed by desert, grew rich on trade, and Buddhist monasteries rose there with merchant money. Monks learned the local languages, and the oases became schools and way stations. The caves carved and painted along these routes still show donors in their best clothes, kneeling beside the Buddha. Fourth, why it worked. A merchant needs trust, a safe night, and a blessing for the road. A monk needs food, company, and a way across the desert. Each gave the other what they lacked. So, as historians tell it, the teaching didn't arrive in China by army. Much of it walked in, one caravan at a time, beside the people carrying silk the other way.
screen: `A WEB OF ROADS, NOT ONE ROAD.` · `TWO MERCHANTS MEET THE BUDDHA.` · `MONASTERIES AT THE OASES.` · `EACH GAVE WHAT THE OTHER LACKED.` · then, large: `MONKS WITH MERCHANTS.`

901.title: The first translators
901.hook: An Shigao and others begin translating into Chinese in Luoyang
901.howItsDone: Buddhists in China, Korea and Japan read the sutras in classical Chinese translations, and teachers often explain the translators' word choices when they teach a text.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the bhikkhu on the Silk Road, walking at the back of the caravans. Your line: monks with merchants. Today the monks reach the city and face a new problem.

How do you say nirvana in a language that has no word for it? That was the job waiting in Luoyang, a great Chinese capital, when monks from the west arrived with texts in their heads and on their backs. The city had readers and writers enough. What it lacked were words: Chinese had no ready words for karma, for rebirth, for a monk's rule. Every sentence was a bridge someone had to build. Today, the first translators.
screen: `NO WORD FOR NIRVANA.` → `A CAPITAL CALLED LUOYANG.` → `EVERY SENTENCE A BRIDGE.`

segments.voice: First, a name: An Shigao. The An in his name marked him, in Chinese records, as coming from Parthia, far to the west. Tradition says he was a prince who gave the throne to an uncle and became a monk. In Luoyang he translated texts on meditation and the breath, on counting breaths and watching the mind. Second, he wasn't alone. Another monk, Lokakshema, from the Kushan lands, translated some of the early Mahayana sutras, and others joined them. The work was done in teams: a foreign monk recited or read the text, someone turned it into spoken Chinese, and a Chinese scribe wrote it down and polished it. Third, the hard part: the words. Where Chinese had no word, translators sometimes borrowed one from Chinese thought. Some used dao, the way, a word from the Chinese classics, for the Buddhist path. Others sounded the foreign word out in Chinese syllables. Both choices had a cost. A borrowed word brought its old meanings with it, and a sounded-out word meant nothing until someone explained it. Fourth, why it matters. The Chinese Buddhist texts read in China, Korea and Japan today come out of a long line of choices like these, made by people working between languages, at a table, one sentence at a time.
screen: `AN SHIGAO, FROM PARTHIA.` · `TEAMS AT THE TABLE.` · `BORROW A WORD OR SOUND IT OUT.` · `CHOICES STILL READ TODAY.` · then, large: `INTO CHINESE.`

segments.voice: Take a simple teaching about the breath: breathing in, know that you are breathing in; breathing out, know that you are breathing out. Say it two or three ways, as you would to a twelve-year-old or a friend at the kitchen table, and notice what each version gains and loses. Then let the words go and rest with one breath at a time, the way An Shigao's breath texts describe it.
An Shigao. A monk from Parthia who translated texts on meditation and the breath in Luoyang, building Chinese words where none existed.

902.title: The White Horse Temple
902.hook: the legend of an emperor's dream and sutras carried on a white horse
902.howItsDone: The White Horse Temple near Luoyang is still an active monastery, and Buddhist pilgrims visit it as a place remembered for the coming of the teaching to China.

segments.voice: Yesterday: An Shigao and the first translators in Luoyang, building Chinese words for ideas that had none. Your line: into Chinese. Today, the story Chinese Buddhists tell about how it all arrived.

An emperor wakes in the night. In his dream a tall golden figure, shining, flew in front of his palace. In the morning he asks his ministers what it means. One of them has heard of a sage in the far west, called the Buddha, who could rise into the air and whose body shone like gold. The emperor sends envoys west to find out more. That's how the legend begins. It ends with a white horse walking slowly into Luoyang.
screen: `A GOLDEN FIGURE IN A DREAM.` → `A SAGE IN THE WEST.` → `ENVOYS SENT TO FIND HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the dream. The emperor in the story is Ming of the Han, and the golden figure is the spark: he wanted to know, so he sent people to ask. Second, the return. The envoys came back with two monks from the west, and with them came sutras and images, loaded on a white horse. Third, the temple. The emperor had a monastery built for the monks outside Luoyang, and named it for the horse that had carried the teaching: the White Horse Temple. A temple by that name still stands near Luoyang, and Chinese tradition remembers it as the place where the teaching first settled in the land. Tradition says the two monks translated a short sutra there. Fourth, how to hold a legend. Historians read this story carefully. They point out that Buddhists were already in China, among traders and foreigners, before the story's date, and that the account was written down later. So they treat it as a legend, not a record. But a legend tells you something a record can't: how people wanted to remember a beginning. Notice its shape. The teaching isn't seized, or preached at the gates. It's asked for, in a dream, and carried in, patiently, by an animal that doesn't know what it carries, with the monks walking beside it.

903.title: Kumarajiva
903.hook: the translator who put the Lotus, Diamond and Vimalakirti into Chinese that people still read
903.tomorrow: The tongue that did not burn
903.howItsDone: In Chinese, Korean, Vietnamese and Japanese temples, Kumarajiva's versions of the Lotus Sutra and the Diamond Sutra are chanted in services and studied in classes.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ming's dream, and the legend of sutras carried into Luoyang on a horse's back. Your line: carried in. Today, a translator whose Chinese is still read aloud.

All conditioned things are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew, like lightning. That is the closing verse of the Diamond Sutra as it's chanted in Chinese in East Asian temples. The Chinese they chant comes from a translation made in Chang'an, by a team gathered around one monk born in an oasis town on the Silk Road. Quick pictures, each gone almost as soon as it appears, set down in a Chinese that still sounds clear. His name was Kumarajiva.
screen: `A DREAM, A BUBBLE, DEW, LIGHTNING.` → `CHANTED IN CHINESE.` → `ONE TRANSLATOR.`

segments.voice: First, where he came from. His biography says he was born in Kucha, one of those oasis towns, to a mother from the royal family and a father from India. He became a monk as a boy and studied in Kashmir. He knew the texts, and he came to know Chinese. Second, the long wait. When a Chinese army took Kucha, Kumarajiva was carried off by a general and held for years in a frontier town. There, some readers think, his Chinese grew strong. Third, the work. A later ruler brought him to the capital, Chang'an, and gave him a large team of monks and scholars. Kumarajiva would hold the text, speak it in Chinese and discuss the hard words with the team, and the scribes would write. From that room came the Lotus Sutra, the Diamond Sutra and the Vimalakirti Sutra in the versions still chanted and studied. Fourth, his way of translating. His biography tells a story: he said that turning Sanskrit into Chinese is like chewing rice before feeding it to someone. The flavor is lost, and the food may even turn the stomach. He knew what translation costs. Even so, his versions read as clear, flowing Chinese that people could actually say aloud, and some readers credit that clarity for how long they've lasted. So the week closes: old texts read again, a southern road, monks with merchants, translators at a table, a white horse, and now the translator whose words people still say.
screen: `BORN IN KUCHA.` · `HELD FOR YEARS ON THE FRONTIER.` · `A TEAM IN CHANG'AN.` · `CHEWED RICE: WHAT IS LOST.` · then, large: `THE TRANSLATOR.`

segments.voice: Say the six pictures from the hook aloud once, giving each its own pause: a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, dew, lightning. Then let each out-breath be one of them, let it go, and start again.
Kumarajiva. The monk from Kucha whose Chinese translations of the Lotus, the Diamond and the Vimalakirti Sutras are still read and chanted.
Your line: the translator. Something is always lost, and still the words carry. That's the week.

fork.setup: you're Kumarajiva. a phrase in the Sanskrit is exact but would sound clumsy in Chinese. what do you do?
options: keep it word for word, however it sounds.
make it clear Chinese that people can read, even if some flavor is lost.
leave the phrase out.
fork.reveal: his versions read as clear, readable Chinese. his chewed-rice saying admits what is lost, and his versions are the ones people still chant.

what it means: he was the translator whose Chinese versions of the Lotus, Diamond and Vimalakirti Sutras are still read.
what a scholar hears: his teams' Chinese leans toward readability over literalness, and his versions stayed in use even where later, more literal translations were made.

chat.says: Why are Kumarajiva's translations still chanted after so long?
options: Some readers credit his clear, flowing Chinese, made with a team, that people could say aloud.
Because he translated word for word, so nothing of the original was ever lost.
Because he wrote those sutras himself, in Chinese, with no source to follow.
chat.meaning: His versions read as clear, flowing Chinese that people could say aloud, and some readers credit that for how long they've lasted. He knew something is lost.
